opus-5.5.text:
I think it's going to be one of the defining technologies of the next decade, honestly. Right now we're in this strange position where we've built these incredibly capable systems, and we fundamentally don't understand how they work. We train them, we poke at them from the outside, we run evals, but the actual computation happening inside is still largely a black box. That's a pretty unusual situation for any engineering discipline to be in.

The way I think about it, interpretability is to neural networks what something like microscopy was to biology. Before you could look inside the cell, you could observe behavior and run experiments, but you couldn't really understand mechanisms. Once you could see inside, it opened up entirely new ways to intervene, design, and fix things. I think we're at that inflection point with AI.

So broadly, I see it shaping things on a few fronts. One is safety and reliability. If you're going to deploy these models in high-stakes settings, in healthcare, finance, critical infrastructure, you want to know *why* a model is doing what it's doing, not just that it passed some benchmark. Being able to detect things like deception, or a model relying on a spurious feature, before it causes harm is enormously valuable.

Second is control. Right now, if you want to change a model's behavior, your main levers are prompting and fine-tuning, which are pretty blunt instruments. Interpretability lets you reach in and steer specific concepts or features directly. That's a much more precise way to shape behavior, and I think it'll become a standard part of how people build with models.

And third, and this is the one I find most exciting, is scientific discovery. These models are learning things about the world, especially models trained on biological or scientific data, that we as humans might not know yet. If we can actually read out what they've learned, we can extract new knowledge from them. That's a completely different relationship with AI than just using it as a tool.

So my view is that interpretability isn't a niche research subfield. Ultimately it's going to be core infrastructure for how we design, debug, and trust every serious AI system.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts understanding a model’s internals with treating it as a black box, then says interpretability will be core infrastructure for designing, debugging, and trusting every serious AI system. This conveys its broad value wherever insight into the system is preferred.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think interpretability is going to end up being one of the load-bearing pieces of how AI actually gets deployed in the world, not a niche research curiosity off to the side.

The way I'd frame it: right now we have these systems that are incredibly capable, but we fundamentally don't understand why they do what they do. We train them, we evaluate them on benchmarks, we poke at them with prompts, and then we ship them. That works okay when the stakes are low. It doesn't work when you want to put a model in charge of something that matters, like medical decisions, financial systems, or critical infrastructure. In every other engineering discipline, we don't accept "it seems to work when we test it" as the bar. We want to understand the mechanism. Interpretability is how we get there for neural networks.

So I see it shaping a few things. First, safety and trust. If you can actually look inside a model and see what concepts it's representing, what it's "thinking" as it produces an answer, you can catch problems that behavioral testing would miss. A model might give the right answer for the wrong reason, or be representing something internally that it isn't saying. That's the kind of thing you only find by looking at the internals.

Second, I think it changes how we build and improve models. Today, when a model does something wrong, the fix is mostly "add more data and retrain" or "tweak the prompt." That's slow and imprecise. If you understand the circuits involved, you can intervene directly, steer the model, or diagnose exactly what went wrong. It turns model development from alchemy into something closer to engineering.

And third, more speculatively, I think interpretability is going to matter for the regulatory and governance side. If governments and companies are going to make decisions about what models are allowed to do, they're going to want evidence that goes beyond "we ran some evals." Being able to say "here's what the model represents internally, here's how we verified it" is a much stronger foundation.

The honest caveat is that the field is still early. We've had real wins, things like identifying interpretable features inside large models, but we're nowhere near a full understanding of a frontier model. There's a race between how fast capabilities are advancing and how fast our understanding is catching up. My bet is that it's worth investing heavily to close that gap, because the alternative is deploying increasingly powerful systems that are essentially black boxes, and I don't think that's a world anyone wants.

r001.rationale: The response presents interpretability as a way to understand AI internals and contrasts that with deploying systems as black boxes, framing it as broadly important to AI deployment.

astra-6.text:
I think it could shape almost every part of how we build and use AI. Right now, we can observe what a model does, but we often have a much weaker understanding of why it does it. Interpretability gives us a way to start closing that gap.

That matters for safety, because we want to understand failures before they become consequential. But it also matters for making models better—for figuring out what they’ve learned, where they’re relying on shortcuts, and how to improve them.

The caveat is that an explanation isn’t automatically a guarantee. We need to test whether our understanding actually lets us predict and change a model’s behavior. If we can do that reliably, interpretability could become a core part of AI engineering.

r001.rationale: The response says interpretability could shape almost every part of AI and help explain model behavior, but it does not state that it could help wherever a white-box approach is preferred over a black-box approach.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it could be foundational. As AI systems become more capable, we’re going to want more than evidence that they usually give good answers. We’ll want to understand how they arrive at those answers, when they might fail, and whether we can change their behavior reliably.

Interpretability could help with all of that, from debugging models to evaluating safety. The part I’m especially interested in is whether it becomes a tool for discovery: can understanding what a model has learned teach us something we didn’t already know?

But understanding one part of a model doesn’t mean we understand the whole system. So I see interpretability as an important part of the toolkit, alongside behavioral testing and monitoring. The real test is whether those insights help us make better decisions about building and deploying AI.

r001.rationale: The response says interpretability can help with understanding model reasoning, debugging, safety evaluation, and discovery, but it does not state that it could help wherever a white-box approach is preferred over a black-box approach.
